catalyst.action: Buy the no-change leg at 54c or better, sized as a lottery ticket at 1%. Cut it if both the Sep 4 payrolls and the Sep 11 CPI run hot — two hot prints is the scenario that makes a September move easy, and there is no reason to hold through the second one to find out.

thesis: The edge is timing, not direction, and it is thin. September is an SEP meeting: a chair who has publicly abolished forward guidance still has to publish a dot plot, and a hawkish dot plot is the way to signal a tightening path without spending a hike at his first meeting — hold-and-signal is the cheapest option Warsh owns. He also stopped short of signalling September specifically, and the analyst reading of the same speech is that the hike arrives in October or December. The Oct leg trades at just 28c, so the market itself does not think tightening is urgent; it thinks it is imminent, which is a different claim. I put September nearer 40-45% against the 47c on offer.

Warsh was also more hawkish than the first headlines conveyed: he said the labour market is effectively at full employment and that financial conditions may not be restraining the economy much at all, which is close to saying policy is not tight enough. The Sep 4 payrolls and Sep 11 CPI can end it. Sized at 1% because of all of this.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is simply that the better-capitalised market disagrees with me: fed funds futures, which are traded by people who hedge real rate risk, sit 9-12 points more hawkish than this contract. Treating that gap as my edge rather than as my error is the exact reasoning that keeps losing trades open. The response is not that I am right, it is that the position is now sized as a 1% lottery ticket with a defined maximum loss and a hard exit if both September prints run hot.

counter_argument: The strongest case against is that the sell side is right and I am buying a value trap with a good story — consensus is Hold with a $14.38 target, 10.6% *below* the market, and analysts covering this name have watched the category shrink for a decade.
